question: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: Young published her single-author 1924 paper on the excretory apparatus in Paramecium while working with Ernest Just at Howard University and at Woods Hole.
After Ernest Just left Howard, Young took on much of the department's teaching load, and her own research time was substantially reduced.
Roger Arliner Young, who lived from 1899 to 1964, studied the contractile vacuole system of Paramecium and the effects of radiation on marine egg cells.

Recent historians argue that the standard narrative of Young's career, fixed on her later setbacks, has obscured her early Paramecium and radiation work — the first single-author zoology papers by an African American woman — recoverable only by reading the archival record alongside the published one.

explanation: The correct answer is D. The goal is to emphasize the corrective contribution of recent historians' work on Young. D states that contribution: the standard narrative, fixed on her later setbacks, has obscured the importance of her early Paramecium and radiation work as the first single-author zoology papers by an African American woman, and recovering it requires reading the archival record alongside the published literature. A and C report Young's publications and research topics but say nothing about what recent historians have done. B foregrounds exactly the later-setbacks material that the corrective work argues has been overemphasized, illustrating the framing being corrected rather than the correction.

studentNotes.intro: While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
bullets: Roger Arliner Young (1899-1964) was a zoologist who studied the contractile vacuole system of Paramecium and the effects of radiation on marine egg cells.
She published her single-author 1924 paper on the excretory apparatus in Paramecium while working with Ernest Just at Howard University and at the Marine Biological Laboratory at Woods Hole.
After Just left Howard, Young carried much of the department's teaching load and saw her own research time substantially reduced.
Recent historians of science argue that the standard narrative of Young's career — focused on her later setbacks — has obscured the importance of her early Paramecium and radiation work.
On this account, that work includes the first single-author research papers in zoology by an African American woman.
Recovering it requires reading the Howard and Woods Hole archival record alongside the published literature, since institutional pressures shaped what she could publish under her own name.
studentNotes.goal: The student wants to emphasize the corrective contribution of recent historians' work on Young.
